name: English
h1: The label your apps came without.
tagline: See what your apps can reach and how much they send. Then limit it.
lead: On your own phone, through Android’s own settings. No internet access, no account, no root.
label_fine: *Known names only. A renamed or hidden SDK is missed, so finding nothing is not proof that nothing is there.
checks_lead: Every line on the label comes from your own phone.
needs_usage: Usage access, if you allow it
checks: Every installed app: where it came from, its sensitive permissions, and the special access that lets an app read the screen or act for you.
The code of every app is read on the phone and matched against the εxodus tracker list, and our own list of SDKs that share your connection, give remote support or record the screen.
VPN, proxy and circumvention apps are compared with their developers’ official signing keys. A copy is called modified only on firm evidence; an unknown key is shown, without a warning.
USB and wireless debugging, certificate authorities you installed, the security patch, and the boot state from the phone’s hardware.
What each app received and sent on mobile data and Wi-Fi in the last 30 or 7 days, and how much of it in the background, from Android’s own count.
Apps you have not opened for 90 days that still hold a permission, special access or background data.
Read the count, use the app, read again, and see how much it sent while you only watched or scrolled.
limits_title: What it sees, and what it can’t
legend_dash: Dashed lines: what this version can’t see.
parts: What you type, and encrypted content
limits: The scan looks for known names, so an SDK that is renamed, obfuscated or loaded later is missed. Finding nothing is not proof that nothing is there.
This version counts how much, not to whom. That is planned for v0.2, in a separate app called Datapavan Watch.
It cannot read encrypted content or what you type inside an app, and it will never try to decrypt anything.
No app can control them, or clean a phone that is already compromised. It finds the risk and guides you.
nc_label: No connection: Datapavan has no internet permission.
plan_title: What you can do with it
plan_body: A short plan, starting with the changes that remove the most risk. Each one opens the right Android screen, where you decide. Datapavan changes nothing itself.
levels: Apps that can control the phone, and apps not opened for 90 days that still hold a sensor, special access or VPN permission.
Also apps that can install apps, traffic sharing, USB debugging, and the other access of apps not opened for 90 days.
Also preinstalled apps, which Datapavan has not tested on your phone.
plan_more: Records what actually changed, notices when a change comes back, and offers undo.
Leaves alone the apps your phone needs, such as your default apps and keyboard.
never_body: Android enforces this. An app without the internet permission cannot open a network connection. Genuine Datapavan never asks for it, and a copy that asks is not genuine.
compare_note: By kind of tool, since each does a different job. Datapavan 0.1 looks and guides; it does not block. Checked in November 2026 against εxodus, AppCensus, TrackerControl, RethinkDNS, NetGuard, DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection, AdGuard, AFWall+ and Android 15 and 16.
compare_rows: Checks a VPN app is the official one
Takes your phone’s one VPN slot
faq: No. It has no permission to use the internet, so it cannot open a network connection. What it finds stays on the phone unless you share it yourself.
Will it work next to my VPN?
Yes. This version does not use Android’s VPN slot, so your VPN or circumvention tool keeps running as it is.
Not in this version. You make each change in Android’s settings. Blocking is planned for v0.3.
Why does it ask for usage access?
To read how much data each app used and when it was last on screen. You can refuse, and the rest still works. Only totals are read, and nothing is kept.
Which phones does it run on?
Phones from any maker with Android 10 or newer, 64-bit or 32-bit, with or without Google services. It is tested from Android 11.
Yes. It is free software under the Apache License 2.0, with no ads and no data sales.
Who makes it? Has anyone audited it?
One maintainer so far, and the code is public. Nothing has been independently audited yet.
get_body: Version 0.1.2 is the first release for everyone. F-Droid and IzzyOnDroid will list it once they have reviewed it.
get_changes: What is new in this version:
get_install: Android asks you to allow installing from your browser; you can turn that off again afterwards. Then, in the app’s settings, “Is this copy genuine?” checks your copy.
get_blocked: If the download does not start, your network may be blocking it. Try GitHub instead, or ask someone you trust to send you the file. A copy from anywhere is fine once its key matches the one shown here.
get_older: Earlier versions, each with its signed notes, are on GitHub.
channels: The signed APK, its SHA-256 and the signed release notes.
The same key on every channel.

news_lead: What has happened in this field, and what it means for someone with an Android phone.
names_lead: Both names come from Old Persian, the language of the Achaemenid kings, known almost only from inscriptions carved in stone about 2,500 years ago.
names: Dāta means law, what has been set down. It appears in Darius I's inscription at Behistun, and lives on in Persian as dād, justice. Pāvan means guardian: it is in xšaçapāvan, protector of the realm, the title that reached English as satrap. The compound itself is ours, built from those two attested parts. That data means data in English is deliberate wordplay, not a shared origin.

The word comes from Xerxes I's inscription on the Gate of All Nations at Persepolis, which speaks of this gateway of all nations. The inscription is in three languages, and guardians stand at the gate's doorways. We chose the name for a planned foundation that belongs to no single nation or company. That the name opens with visa in English is wordplay too, not a shared origin: this gateway of all nations asks no one for a visa.
